topic: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
parentTitle: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
title: Carers, families and community mental health services
blurb: Work in a Triangle of Care with service users and carers, share information lawfully, and use crisis and community services well.
question: Mrs Begum phones the community team. Her son Imran, 27, who has schizophrenia, has asked staff not to share details of his care with her. She is frightened because he has stopped eating and talks about 'ending things'. What should the nurse do?

teach.body: Carers (often family) provide much of the day-to-day support for people with mental illness and often notice relapse first. The Triangle of Care (Carers Trust) describes a therapeutic alliance between the service user, the professional and the carer that promotes safety, supports recovery and sustains wellbeing. Plain English: involve the people who are there at 3 am, listen to them, and support them too.
teach.cite: Carers Trust, Triangle of Care; NICE CG178 1.1.4.1-1.1.4.4

teach.caption: All three share information and decisions as far as the person agrees.

teach.h: Triangle of Care: six key standards
head: Standard
rows: Carers and their role identified at first contact or as soon as possible
Staff are 'carer aware' and trained in carer engagement
Protocols on confidentiality and sharing information
A carer introduction to the service, with information across the pathway
A range of carer support services
teach.caption: Carers Trust. Carers also have a legal right to a carer's assessment (Care Act 2014 s10).

rows.label: General info
values: About the illness, services, crisis help

rows.label: Personal info
values: If risk of serious harm overrides confidentiality
Details of his care and treatment

teach.caption: Code 5.4: share only when safety and public protection override confidentiality. CG178 1.1.4.2: negotiate early how information is shared, stressing risk.

steps.label: Crisis resolution and home treatment
steps.sub: First line in an acute episode

steps.label: Inpatient admission
steps.sub: When home care is not safe

teach.caption: CG178 1.4.1.1-1.4.1.3: CRHT teams are first line and the gateway to acute care; consider acute community treatment before admission.

items: Give carers written and verbal information on the illness, recovery, carer support, services and how to get help in a crisis.
Negotiate information sharing early, and review it regularly.
Offer a carer-focused education and support programme as early as possible, with a positive message about recovery.
Tell carers about their right to a carer's assessment, and include young carers.

teach.body: The nurse listens fully: hearing a carer never breaches confidentiality. Mrs Begum reports suicidal talk and not eating, so the nurse acts on the risk at once: she arranges an urgent assessment of Imran, involving the crisis resolution and home treatment team, and records the information. She gives Mrs Begum general information and crisis numbers. Without Imran's consent she does not share details of his treatment, unless risk of serious harm makes disclosure necessary, and she revisits consent with him.

teach.text: Confidentiality does not stop you LISTENING to carers or giving them general information and crisis contacts. Refusing even to hear a carer's concerns is a common failure. Equally, a person's refusal to share does not end the discussion: revisit it, and share personal details without consent only when safety overrides confidentiality.

items: Triangle of Care: service user, carer and professional in partnership; six key standards.
Always listen to carers; give general information; share personal details with consent unless risk overrides.
Family intervention: at least 10 sessions over 3-12 months; carer education programme early.
CRHT teams are first line in an acute episode in the community; follow up within 7 days of discharge (48 h if suicide risk).

summary: You can now apply the Triangle of Care and share information with carers lawfully, always listening and giving general information. You can also place crisis resolution, home treatment and family intervention correctly in community mental health care.

A.q: A carer phones to share concerns about her husband, who has not consented to information sharing. What may the nurse do?
options: End the call to protect his confidentiality
Listen to her concerns and record them
Share his full care plan to reassure her
Ask her to put her concerns in writing first
A.why: Listening to a carer does not breach confidentiality; the information can be recorded and acted on, while personal details are not disclosed without consent unless risk overrides.

whyNot.0: Refusing to listen loses vital information about risk.
whyNot.2: Sharing his care plan without consent breaches confidentiality.
whyNot.3: A delay risks missing urgent concerns.

A.q: Under NICE CG178, how many planned sessions should family intervention for psychosis include as a minimum?
options: 4 sessions
6 sessions
10 sessions
16 sessions
A.why: CG178 1.3.7.2: family intervention should include at least 10 planned sessions over 3 months to 1 year.

whyNot.3: 16 sessions is the minimum for CBTp, not family intervention.

A.q: Which service does NICE CG178 describe as first line for supporting a person with an acute episode of psychosis in the community when other teams cannot manage the risk?
options: Crisis resolution and home treatment team
NHS Talking Therapies service
A community assertive outreach day centre
The GP practice nurse team
A.why: CG178 1.4.1.1: offer crisis resolution and home treatment teams as a first-line service during an acute episode when the severity or risk exceeds other community teams' capacity.

whyNot.1: Talking Therapies treat common mental health problems, not acute psychosis.
whyNot.2: This is not the CG178 first-line crisis service.
whyNot.3: Primary care cannot provide acute crisis treatment.

B.q: Which is the first of the Triangle of Care's six key standards?
options: A range of carer support services is available
Defined posts responsible for carers are in place
Carers are identified at first contact or soon after
Carers sign the care plan alongside the patient
B.why: Standard 1: carers and the essential role they play are identified at first contact, or as soon as possible thereafter.

whyNot.3: This is not one of the six standards.

B.q: Mr Evans cares for his wife, who has bipolar disorder. He is exhausted and has stopped working. What should the nurse tell him?
options: He has a right to a carer's assessment
Support is available once his wife consents
Carers' needs are assessed by the GP practice
He must apply for his wife's benefits first
B.why: Under the Care Act 2014 s10, carers have a right to a carer's assessment of their own needs, independent of the cared-for person's consent.

whyNot.1: A carer's assessment is his right and does not depend on her consent.
whyNot.2: Carer's assessments are a local authority duty under the Care Act, not a GP one.
whyNot.3: Benefit applications are not a precondition.

B.q: Lucy, 32, is discharged from an acute ward. Her team identified a raised suicide risk. When does NICE NG53 say she should be followed up?
options: Within 7 days, as for every discharge
Within 14 days, at her first outpatient visit
Within 72 hours of leaving the ward
Within 48 hours of discharge
B.why: NG53 1.6.8: follow up within 48 hours of discharge if a risk of suicide has been identified; otherwise within 7 days (1.6.7).

whyNot.0: 7 days is the standard where no suicide risk has been identified.
whyNot.2: 72 hours is not the NG53 timescale.

C.q: Imran tells the nurse he does not want his mother told anything about his care. His mother reports he has stopped eating and talks of 'ending things'. Which action best balances confidentiality and safety?
options: Note the call and wait, as he has refused consent
Tell his mother everything in his notes
Act urgently on the risk and revisit consent with him
Ask his mother to persuade him to accept help at home
C.why: Information from carers must be acted on: arrange urgent assessment. Personal details are shared without consent only if risk of serious harm overrides confidentiality (Code 5.4), and consent should be revisited.

whyNot.0: Waiting on reported suicide risk is unsafe; it must be acted on now.
whyNot.1: Full disclosure goes beyond what any risk justifies.
whyNot.3: This passes responsibility for risk management to the carer.

C.q: Tom, 24, has a relapse of psychosis. He wants to stay at home and his parents are willing to help. Risk is moderate and manageable with daily visits. What does NICE CG178 support?
options: Admission to an inpatient unit straight away
A crisis house far from his family
Waiting for his next routine CMHT outpatient review
Acute care from the crisis and home treatment team
C.why: CG178 1.4.1.1-1.4.1.3: CRHT teams are first line in an acute episode and acute community treatment should be considered before admission.

whyNot.0: Admission is for when home treatment is not safe or suitable.
whyNot.1: Crisis houses depend on preference and need; distance from family is a disadvantage.
whyNot.2: A relapse needs prompt acute care, not routine review.

C.q: Jo's family say they want to learn how to help when her voices get worse, and Jo agrees. What should the team offer under NICE CG178?
options: A single information leaflet about psychosis
Family intervention of at least 10 sessions
A referral to a carers' charity in place of care
Individual CBT for her mother in place of Jo's
C.why: CG178 1.3.7.2: offer family intervention (at least 10 sessions over 3-12 months, including Jo where practical) with negotiated problem solving and crisis management, plus carer education and support.

whyNot.0: A leaflet is part of information-giving, not family intervention.
whyNot.2: Charities can add support but do not replace NICE-recommended family intervention.
whyNot.3: Family intervention involves the family together with Jo.

reteach.title: Listen always, share wisely
reteach.question: What can you do for a carer when the person has not consented to sharing?

blocks.h: Three things you can always do
blocks.body: 1. Listen and record their concerns. 2. Give general information about the illness, services and how to get help in a crisis. 3. Offer support for the carer in their own right, including a carer's assessment. Personal details of the person's care need consent, unless risk overrides confidentiality.

blocks.text: Hearing a carer never breaches confidentiality.

explain.body: A therapeutic alliance between service user, professional and carer; six standards from identifying carers at first contact to carer support services.

test.q: What does the Triangle of Care describe?
options: A partnership of service user, carer and professional
A three-step tool for scoring carer stress
The three statutory duties of the nearest relative
Three levels of observation on an inpatient ward
test.why: The Triangle of Care is a therapeutic alliance between service user, staff member and carer that promotes safety, recovery and wellbeing.

whyNot.1: It is not a scoring tool.
whyNot.2: Nearest relative duties come from the MHA, not the Triangle of Care.

explain.body: Always listen; give general information; share personal details with consent, or without it only when risk of serious harm overrides confidentiality (Code 5.4).

test.q: Without a service user's consent, which information can the nurse give his carer?
options: His medication doses and side effects
The content of his last ward round
How to contact the crisis team
His risk assessment in full
test.why: General information such as how to get help in a crisis can be given without breaching confidentiality (CG178 1.1.4.1).

whyNot.1: Ward round content is personal information.
whyNot.3: Disclosing his full risk assessment needs consent unless serious risk overrides.

explain.body: At least 10 planned sessions over 3 months to 1 year, including the person where practical; problem solving and crisis management.

test.q: Over what period does NICE CG178 say family intervention should be delivered?
options: Within 2 weeks
Between 3 months and 1 year
Over 2 to 3 years
In a single day workshop
test.why: CG178 1.3.7.2: family intervention should be carried out for between 3 months and 1 year, with at least 10 planned sessions.

whyNot.3: A single workshop is not family intervention.

explain.body: CRHT teams are first line in an acute episode in the community and the gateway to acute care; consider acute community treatment before admission. Follow up within 7 days of discharge (48 h if suicide risk).

test.q: According to NICE CG178, what role do crisis resolution and home treatment teams have in acute care?
options: They provide long-term psychotherapy
They replace the need for any inpatient admission beds
They manage annual physical health checks
They are the single point of entry to acute services
test.why: CG178 1.4.1.2: CRHT teams should be the single point of entry to all other acute services in the community and in hospitals.

whyNot.2: Physical health monitoring sits with secondary and primary care teams.
